element: Heye et al. (Supporting Artifact Evaluation with LLMs: A Study with Published Security Research Papers, arXiv:2603.06862)

UC1.note: No stage produces any appendix or venue-format document; outputs are scores, a container, and logs.

UC3.evidence: "(ii) detect potential inconsistencies between claims and submitted artifacts" (Sec. I, p.1)
UC3.note: Intro promises claim/artifact inconsistency detection but no stage actually produces claim-to-component links; RATE/ASSESS are concept-vector scores, PREPARE only runs code.

UC4.evidence: "The final deliverable of this stage is either a runnable container image ... or a structured error report that pinpoints issues the agent faced." (Sec. III-C, p.4)
UC4.note: PREPARE reports setup failures (missing deps, bad links) and RATE scores Readme quality, but neither is relative to an explicit standard S; partial is right.

UC5.evidence: "The classifier outputs which pitfalls are most likely present. The report highlights potential design or evaluation flaws, providing reviewers with insights" (Sec. III-D, p.4)
UC5.note: ASSESS flags methodological gaps in the paper text (e.g. lab-only evaluation, inappropriate baseline/threat model from Arp et al.'s taxonomy), which is a partial form of reporting what the paper lacks; current 0 seems too low.

UC6.evidence: "The final deliverable of this stage is either a runnable container image ready for further analysis by an AE expert" (Sec. III-C, p.4)
UC6.note: PREPARE autonomously generates an execution environment (Docker container) as a deliverable, but from A+Readme+P rather than from P alone, so at most partial; current 0 is debatable.

UC7.evidence: "we derive a unique concept vector for each pitfall individually using a set of training papers" (Sec. III-D, p.4)
UC7.note: Training papers are used to fit concept vectors/classifiers, not to present exemplar comparisons to a user.

B1.evidence: "we aim to provide automated support for reviewers of scientific contributions to improve the scalability of AE" (Sec. I, p.1)

B2.evidence: "The LLM-based agent used in this stage iteratively issues shell commands to clone the repository, install dependencies, and compile and execute code" (Sec. III-A, p.3)
B2.note: PREPARE executes code in Docker; RATE and ASSESS are text-only hidden-state projections, so 4 rather than 5.

B3.evidence: "the full paper text and, in the case of RATE, a Readme file associated with the submission's code artifact" (Sec. IV-B, p.4)
B3.note: RATE takes paper+Readme, ASSESS paper only, PREPARE the codebase+paper; genuinely mixed.

B4.evidence: "We focus on Arp et al.'s [35] taxonomy of ten common pitfalls in AI-driven cybersecurity research" (Sec. III-D, p.4)
B4.note: ASSESS is explicitly driven by a published pitfall taxonomy and RATE is trained against Olszewski's reproducibility labels, though no venue badging standard is encoded; 3 fits better than 2.

B5.evidence: "The resulting score s reflects how strongly the paper's text aligns with the distilled reproducibility concept vector" (Sec. III-B, p.4)
B5.note: Outputs are scores/binary classifications plus a container and a structured error log; no prose report.

disagreements: UC5: current 0, should be 1 because ASSESS delivers a per-paper report of methodological pitfalls present in the paper text (lab-only evaluation, inappropriate baseline, etc.), a partial form of 'what the paper lacks'.
UC6: current 0, arguably 1 because PREPARE's deliverable is an autonomously generated runnable container image (environment material), though it starts from A+Readme rather than P alone.
B4: current 2, arguably 3 because ASSESS is explicitly driven by Arp et al.'s published ten-pitfall taxonomy and RATE thresholds are fit to Olszewski's published reproducibility labels.
one_line_summary: Reviewer-facing three-stage pipeline: hidden-state concept vectors score paper+Readme reproducibility, an LLM agent auto-builds Docker environments, and a classifier flags Arp-taxonomy methodological pitfalls in the paper.
